Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Leilani was sixty-six and had run her small convenience store in Honolulu for nearly thirty years. What happened on a Tuesday evening in February had undone her. She had been closing up, counting the register, when a police officer entered, responding to a noise complaint from a neighboring apartment. She remembered the door swinging open, the officer’s hand going to his holster, the way he shouted at her to step away from the counter. She could not remember what happened in the next thirty seconds—only that she ended up on the floor, her wrists twisted behind her back, the cold tile against her cheek, and the officer’s knee pressing into her spine. The charge was later dropped, but the event had already carved itself into her.

Leilani began to feel the weight of it most acutely at dusk. The same time of day, around six in the evening, her chest would tighten and her vision would swim. She would feel dizzy, lightheaded, as though the floor were tilting. When that dizziness hit at dusk, she stopped what she was doing and reached for her phone to buy something online, because the feeling of the floor tilting was unbearable unless she drowned it out with a purchase. Each time dusk arrived and the dizziness rose, she thought to herself that anyone else would have been over this by now, and the thought confirmed what she already feared — that she was a lousy coper, fundamentally inadequate. She had come to believe that her reactions since that night proved she was a lousy coper, that she was fundamentally inadequate for not being able to shake it off. Each time the memory broke through — the door swinging open, the officer's hand — the thought that followed was always the same: that she was broken, and that this proved something permanent about her. That belief — that she was a lousy coper — kept bringing her back to the moment on the floor, because she needed to revisit it to understand exactly where she had become the kind of person who couldn't handle a single Tuesday evening. That belief — that she was somehow broken by what had happened — kept pulling her back into the memory itself, as if she needed to replay it to find the exact moment she had become this person she could not accept. When she felt that dizziness rising, she was certain she was losing her mind, that she was going crazy. It was in those moments, standing behind her register as the light faded, that she would find herself reaching for her phone and buying something online—a new kitchen gadget she did not need, a dress she would never wear. The spending was a way to distract herself, to feel a brief flood of something other than fear.

As the weeks passed, Leilani began avoiding the store at closing time, asking her part-time employee to handle the last hour. She avoided the anniversary of the event entirely, taking a flight to visit her sister on the mainland, telling herself it was just a vacation. Not talking about it, not telling the story to anyone, had kept the memory sealed and untouched — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for months, and that effort had preserved it exactly as it was. She had learned that if she kept moving, kept the television on, or bought something online, the memory couldn't get a foothold — stillness was the enemy, and activity was the only way to keep the fragments at bay. But the effort of keeping the event at a distance had done the opposite — the memory remained sealed and untouched, and when it did surface, it came back with the same raw, fragmented force as the first week, as though no time had passed at all. Not talking about it, not telling the story to anyone, had kept the memory in its original form — unprocessed, unsoftened, exactly as vivid as the night it happened. But the memory refused to stay buried. The story felt unreal to her, too extreme to have actually happened, and yet she could not put it into words when her sister asked. The event existed only as a series of fragments—the door, the hand, the floor—and she could not string them together into a coherent narrative. This inability to talk about it reinforced her sense that she was a bad coper, that anyone else would have been able to move on. Because the memory came back in those vivid, wordless fragments, she began to see threads of it everywhere—in the way a customer's hand moved near a counter, in the creak of a door opening, in the particular shade of fluorescent light that reminded her of that evening.

The dizziness itself had become a trigger. Whenever she felt lightheaded—from standing up too fast, from the heat—it pulled her back into that moment on the tile floor, and the memory would surge up, vivid and wordless. She had begun to believe that being watched made it worse. If a customer lingered near the counter, or if she noticed a security camera in a shop window, her stomach would drop. She would leave the store abruptly, telling her employee she felt unwell, and walk home with her head down. The avoidance made her feel temporarily safer, but it also deepened her conviction that she could not handle normal life, that she was falling apart. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. Three months of avoiding the store at dusk had told her something she couldn't argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been able to close up like she used to. And the places she now avoided — the store at dusk, the grocery store aisle, any shop with a security camera — had themselves become reminders; the long list of what she could no longer do was its own daily map of what had happened that Tuesday evening. The long way she walked home to avoid the shop with the security camera, the routes she no longer took, the hours she could no longer work — all of it was a daily geography of the event, each detour a fresh reminder of what she was running from. Each place she avoided became a trigger in itself — the long way she walked home every evening was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened that Tuesday. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop when she felt watched, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. The spending, too, had a cost: her credit card bills were climbing, and she had started hiding packages from her daughter, who visited on weekends.

By the time she sought help, Leilani could no longer ignore the pattern. She had stopped going to the store altogether for three days, claiming she had the flu. What finally brought her to the clinic was a single moment: she had felt dizzy in the grocery store, and for a split second, she had been certain she was about to be thrown to the ground again. She left her cart in the aisle and walked out. She was afraid of what she might do next—how much further she would retreat, how much more she would spend—and she was desperate for the memory to stop feeling so unreal, so that she could finally believe it was over.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Leilani was sixty-six and had run her small convenience store in Honolulu for nearly thirty years. What happened on a Tuesday evening in February had undone her. She had been closing up, counting the register, when a police officer entered, responding to a noise complaint from a neighboring apartment. She remembered the door swinging open, the officer’s hand going to his holster, the way he shouted at her to step away from the counter. She could not remember what happened in the next thirty seconds—only that she ended up on the floor, her wrists twisted behind her back, the cold tile against her cheek, and the officer’s knee pressing into her spine. The charge was later dropped, but the event had already carved itself into her.

Leilani began to feel the weight of it most acutely at dusk. The same time of day, around six in the evening, her chest would tighten and her vision would swim. She would feel dizzy, lightheaded, as though the floor were tilting. When that dizziness hit at dusk, she stopped what she was doing and reached for her phone to buy something online, because the feeling of the floor tilting was unbearable unless she drowned it out with a purchase. Each time dusk arrived and the dizziness rose, she thought to herself that anyone else would have been over this by now, and the thought confirmed what she already feared — that she was a lousy coper, fundamentally inadequate. She had come to believe that her reactions since that night proved she was a lousy coper, that she was fundamentally inadequate for not being able to shake it off. Each time the memory broke through — the door swinging open, the officer's hand — the thought that followed was always the same: that she was broken, and that this proved something permanent about her. That belief — that she was a lousy coper — kept bringing her back to the moment on the floor, because she needed to revisit it to understand exactly where she had become the kind of person who couldn't handle a single Tuesday evening. That belief — that she was somehow broken by what had happened — kept pulling her back into the memory itself, as if she needed to replay it to find the exact moment she had become this person she could not accept. When she felt that dizziness rising, she was certain she was losing her mind, that she was going crazy. It was in those moments, standing behind her register as the light faded, that she would find herself reaching for her phone and buying something online—a new kitchen gadget she did not need, a dress she would never wear. The spending was a way to distract herself, to feel a brief flood of something other than fear.

As the weeks passed, Leilani began avoiding the store at closing time, asking her part-time employee to handle the last hour. She avoided the anniversary of the event entirely, taking a flight to visit her sister on the mainland, telling herself it was just a vacation. Not talking about it, not telling the story to anyone, had kept the memory sealed and untouched — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for months, and that effort had preserved it exactly as it was. She had learned that if she kept moving, kept the television on, or bought something online, the memory couldn't get a foothold — stillness was the enemy, and activity was the only way to keep the fragments at bay. But the effort of keeping the event at a distance had done the opposite — the memory remained sealed and untouched, and when it did surface, it came back with the same raw, fragmented force as the first week, as though no time had passed at all. Not talking about it, not telling the story to anyone, had kept the memory in its original form — unprocessed, unsoftened, exactly as vivid as the night it happened. But the memory refused to stay buried. The story felt unreal to her, too extreme to have actually happened, and yet she could not put it into words when her sister asked. The event existed only as a series of fragments—the door, the hand, the floor—and she could not string them together into a coherent narrative. This inability to talk about it reinforced her sense that she was a bad coper, that anyone else would have been able to move on. Because the memory came back in those vivid, wordless fragments, she began to see threads of it everywhere—in the way a customer's hand moved near a counter, in the creak of a door opening, in the particular shade of fluorescent light that reminded her of that evening.

The dizziness itself had become a trigger. Whenever she felt lightheaded—from standing up too fast, from the heat—it pulled her back into that moment on the tile floor, and the memory would surge up, vivid and wordless. She had begun to believe that being watched made it worse. If a customer lingered near the counter, or if she noticed a security camera in a shop window, her stomach would drop. She would leave the store abruptly, telling her employee she felt unwell, and walk home with her head down. The avoidance made her feel temporarily safer, but it also deepened her conviction that she could not handle normal life, that she was falling apart. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. Three months of avoiding the store at dusk had told her something she couldn't argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been able to close up like she used to. And the places she now avoided — the store at dusk, the grocery store aisle, any shop with a security camera — had themselves become reminders; the long list of what she could no longer do was its own daily map of what had happened that Tuesday evening. The long way she walked home to avoid the shop with the security camera, the routes she no longer took, the hours she could no longer work — all of it was a daily geography of the event, each detour a fresh reminder of what she was running from. Each place she avoided became a trigger in itself — the long way she walked home every evening was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened that Tuesday. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop when she felt watched, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. The spending, too, had a cost: her credit card bills were climbing, and she had started hiding packages from her daughter, who visited on weekends.

By the time she sought help, Leilani could no longer ignore the pattern. She had stopped going to the store altogether for three days, claiming she had the flu. What finally brought her to the clinic was a single moment: she had felt dizzy in the grocery store, and for a split second, she had been certain she was about to be thrown to the ground again. She left her cart in the aisle and walked out. She was afraid of what she might do next—how much further she would retreat, how much more she would spend—and she was desperate for the memory to stop feeling so unreal, so that she could finally believe it was over.
